stories.headline: Pluto Security leaves stealth with $42 million to watch AI agents
stories.standfirst: Pluto Security says about 60% of the AI risks it detects come from vibe-coded tools built by non-developers, with finance staff the biggest source, TechCrunch reported.
body: Pluto Security, a startup that monitors the AI tools, agents and apps employees use at work, has come out of stealth with $42 million in funding, TechCrunch reported on 13 October. The round combines an $8.5 million seed led by TLV Partners and a $34 million Series A led by Jump Capital. No other outlet has reported the figures yet.

The company's own numbers are the most striking part, and they are Pluto's claims rather than independent findings. Chief executive and co-founder Shahar Bahat told TechCrunch that around 60% of the risks Pluto detects across its customers involve tools built by non-developers through vibe coding. Finance departments are the largest source, followed by marketing and legal. Developers rank fourth.

Bahat gave one example: a vibe-coded app built by a finance employee at a Fortune 500 company to manage customer information and churn, which was exposed to the internet. She also said a newly announced AI tool can appear inside a company's environment within two hours of release, and that Pluto found malicious activity in every proof-of-concept deployment, some of it live attacks, according to TechCrunch.

The product watches AI tools, skills, extensions, MCP servers and the apps and agents staff build. TechCrunch says it hooks into endpoint security and device management systems, or runs its own sensors, and collects prompts, commands, running processes and permissions. Pluto says lightweight models on the device judge agent behaviour and can step in mid-task, for instance by blocking an agent that asks for permissions beyond what the user intended.

Pluto began selling in April and says it has passed $2 million in annual recurring revenue with more than 30 enterprise customers, including Oscar Health, Workato, Sixt and AlphaSense. It has 40 employees across the US and Israel. In April it also launched Plutonium, a free scanner for public AI skills, connectors and add-ons, which Bahat says thousands of security professionals use. TechCrunch notes it joins a crowded field that includes Zenity, AIR, InsightFinder and LayerX.

stories.headline: Pulse Local is a Mac budgeting app with its AI models on-device
stories.standfirst: The free Apple Silicon beta downloads about 2.9 GB of small open models and, its maker says, keeps the ledger and chat questions on the machine.
body: Pulse Local, a budgeting app for Apple Silicon Macs, is in beta and runs its chat assistant on small AI models downloaded to the user's own machine. The developer showed it on Hacker News, where the Show HN post had 54 points and 29 comments at the time of reading. Nobody else has reported on it or tested it yet, so what follows is the maker's description from its website.

The page says the app is free with every feature and needs no account. Users can pay a one-time $20, $40 or any amount they choose, and US bank sync through Plaid costs $29 a year for three institutions, with extra institutions at $8 each. Elsewhere, transactions come in by CSV import. A Windows version is planned next, and the chat answers in English only.

The models download once on first start, about 2.9 GB in total. The largest, at 2.5 GB, checks answers about money and can be turned off in settings. The page calls the models small and open and links one tuned model on Hugging Face, but does not name the others. It says the chat answers from the user's own transactions, labels what it included and checks each figure before showing it.

On privacy, the developer says the ledger, the models and the questions never leave the machine. The only regular network request, it says, checks for app updates and carries nothing about the user, and analytics and crash logs are never sent. For bank sync, it says transactions pass through the server's memory without being stored. These are the maker's claims and have not been independently checked.

The page is open about the limits. Small models are weaker than frontier ones on open-ended questions, and a money answer with the checker on takes 12 to 14 seconds. When the two readings disagree, Pulse says it is not sure, according to the page. It also says nothing in the app is financial advice, and Intel Macs are not supported.
